output.summary: KEP-4214 proposes that kubeadm stop binding the admin.conf credential to system:masters. Instead, admin.conf gets a regular cluster-admin credential via a new kubeadm:cluster-admins group, and a separate super-admin.conf holds the break-glass credential bound to system:masters. The KEP is in status implementable, stage alpha.
output.rationale: The system:masters group bypasses RBAC, so its permissions cannot be removed, and Kubernetes lacks certificate revocation. The only way to revoke such a credential is a CA rotation. Splitting the credential lets admin.conf be revoked with RBAC while a break-glass super-admin.conf remains for disruptive cases.

alternatives.why_not: The readme states that a credential bound to system:masters can bypass RBAC and that its permissions cannot be removed, so a compromised admin.conf can only be revoked by CA rotation.

alternatives.option: Use the existing system:masters or kubeadm:cluster-admins groups for additional users
alternatives.why_not: The proposal says using the existing system:masters or kubeadm:cluster-admins Groups will not be recommended; new users should get their own ClusterRoleBinding per User or Group.

evidence.quote: Binding an admin credential to the`system:masters` group means it can [bypass RBAC](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubeadm/issues/2414#issue-836108390) - i.e. its permissions cannot be removed.
A general purpose `admin.conf` must be created that does not bind to `system:masters`. This credential can be shared by kubeadm deployed control plane nodes.
A separate "break-glass", super-user credential can be managed in `super-admin.conf`. This credential can be used to restore the cluster to a normal state in case of disruptive admin user activity.
To preserve the existing behavior where `admin.conf` has full cluster access, a new ClusterRoleBinding will be created called `kubeadm:cluster-admins`.
